title: A Autopsy for the Portrait
premise: Yara Okonkwo, archivist of St. Brannoc's Cathedral, has spent years quietly untangling deaths the police mislabeled as accidents, keeping her findings in a private ledger no one knows exists. When twin letters arrive — one confessing to the drowning of choirboy Elias Wren thirty years ago, one promising that 'the tide will give up what it took' — she realizes the confessor knows about her ledger and is daring her to finish what the law abandoned. Following alibis woven across three decades, she discovers the cathedral's locked crypt hides not a body but proof: a portrait painted over Elias's last known likeness by the man everyone trusted. In the climax, at low tide beneath the sea wall, Yara confronts the aging painter, who confesses fully but begs for mercy outside the law; she must choose between handing him to police or letting him live under the weight of public truth. She chooses exposure without arrest — his name carved into the record, his freedom hollowed out — and buries Elias's restored portrait where the congregation can finally see it.
about_author: Lena Sandoval is a former parish records clerk from the Cornish coast who spent a decade cataloguing centuries of baptismal registers before turning to fiction. Her mysteries are known for their quiet ecclesiastical settings and protagonists who believe justice is a craft practiced in archives, not courtrooms.

chapters.title: The Twin Letters
chapters.summary: Yara Okonkwo, cataloguing the cathedral crypt's sealed inventory, receives two letters postmarked the same day: one confessing to a thirty-year-old drowning, one promising more deaths if she doesn't act. Her POV establishes her secret ledger of solved 'accidents' and her dread that someone is watching. The emotional beat is cold recognition — she has been summoned.

chapters.title: What the Tide Took
chapters.summary: Yara researches the 1994 drowning of choirboy Elias Wren, ruled accidental, and interviews retired verger Tom Pellowe, whose alibi that night was suspiciously precise. Through her POV we feel the pull of belonging — Elias was a boy the parish chose to forget. The beat is grief resurfacing like something washed ashore.

chapters.title: A Portrait Overpainted
chapters.summary: Examining the cathedral's donated portraits, Yara finds an X-ray anomaly beneath a revered painting of Dean Aldous Crane: a smaller figure, a boy's face, painted over. Her POV tightens with forensic excitement. The beat is revelation — the confession letter described this exact canvas before she found it.

chapters.title: Alibis in Amber
chapters.summary: Yara maps the night of Elias's death through old service rosters, discovering three witnesses whose accounts interlock too perfectly — rehearsed. A second threatening letter arrives referencing her ledger by page number. The beat is violation and rising fear: the writer has been inside her office.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Yara obtains the crypt key from the diocesan registrar and finds the chamber empty except for a hidden niche holding Elias's school satchel, preserved and deliberate. Detective Inspector Rhys Calloway, half-aware of her reputation, begins asking questions she can't answer honestly. The beat is the thrill of evidence shadowed by the risk of exposure.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Yara tracks down Miriam Voss, the organist who left the parish abruptly in 1994, now dying in a hospice. Miriam reveals she saw Dean Crane with Elias that night and was paid to stay silent — and that the second letter-writer once wrote to her too. The beat is sorrowful solidarity between keepers of buried things.

chapters.title: The Confessor's Hand
chapters.summary: Handwriting analysis points Yara toward Father Anselm Rook, Crane's former curate, whose sermons quote phrases from both letters verbatim. When she confronts him, he admits sending the confession — not as guilt, but as bait to force her, the unofficial solver, to do what courts never would. The beat is moral vertigo: an ally who manipulated her.

chapters.title: Low Water
chapters.summary: The final letter promises the tide will give up its proof at the spring ebb. Yara and Rook search the mudflats below the sea wall and find a rusted tin box: Elias's shoes, and a photograph placing Crane at the water's edge. Crane appears, having followed them. The beat is dread crystallizing into confrontation.

chapters.title: An Autopsy for the Portrait
chapters.summary: In the crypt, Crane confesses — Elias died fleeing him, and the overpainting was penance and erasure at once. He begs Yara to let him die unaccused, an old man with a legacy intact. Yara, holding the ledger that defines her, weighs law against truth. The beat is the novel's moral crux, rendered in whispered voices among stone saints.

chapters.title: Where the Light Falls
chapters.summary: Yara restores the original portrait and hangs it publicly; Crane resigns in disgrace but faces no trial, living on under the congregation's knowing eyes. She adds a final entry to her ledger — not a solution, but a choice. The beat is bittersweet resolution: justice delivered outside the law, belonging finally granted to a forgotten boy.
